analytic.title: Weight bound Limits in Supertasking Approach for Guaranteed Timeline Constraints

div.p: We investigated the problem of supertasking in Pfairscheduled multiprocessor systems. In this approach, a set of tasks (component tasks) is grouped together to form a supertask, which is then scheduled as an ordinary Pfair task. Whenever a supertask is scheduled, its processor time is allocated to its component tasks according to an internal scheduling algorithm. Supertasking approach does not provide guarantees that its component tasks will respect the timeline constraints.

In this paper, we propose a new condition for constructing a supertask from its component tasks in such a way that all timing constraints of its component tasks are guaranteed without compromising on schedulability loss. This condition is expressed as weight bound relation b/w supertask and its component tasks.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time systems are one of the fields of computing where major benefits are expected from the increasing availability of multiprocessor technology. However, taking full advantage of multiprocessor's capabilities for real-time computing has shown to be difficult. This is mainly due to the fact that scheduling algorithms for multiprocessors are significantly more complex than for uniprocessors.

Scheduling of tasks on multiprocessor systems is typically solved using two different methods based on how tasks are assigned to the processors at run-time; namely partitioning and non-partitioning. In the partitioning-based method, all instances of a task are executed on the same processor which is determined before run-time by a partitioning algorithm. In a non partitioning method, any instance of a task can be executed on a different processor, or even be preempted and moved to a different processor, before it is completed.

Partitioning method have several advantages over non partitioning methods [4,5,6,11,12,13]. Firstly, the scheduling overhead associated with a partitioning method is lower than the overhead associated with a nonpartitioning method. Secondly, partitioning methods allow us to apply well-known uniprocessor scheduling algorithms on each processor. Thirdly and most importantly, each processor could use resources dedicated to it i.e. distributed memory etc. The last mentioned aspect improves the performance of the system a lot and in most cases it proves the partitioning method to be better than its counterpart. Optimal assignment of tasks to processors is known to be NPhard, which is major drawback of partitioning method.

In contrast, the non-partitioning method has received much less attention [2,3,14,15,16], mainly because it is believed to suffer from scheduling and implementation-related shortcomings, also because it lacks support for more advanced system models, such as the management of shared resources. The other important factor that makes this approach of less interest is the use of a shared memory which introduces the bottleneck for system scalability. On the better side, schedulability bounds are much better than its counterpart.

One technique that has the potential to ameliorate these problems is the use of group-based or hierarchical scheduling technique [7,8,9,10]. Under this approach, sets of tasks are scheduled instead of individual tasks. When a set of tasks is selected to execute, an internal scheduler is invoked to distribute the processor time among the individual tasks. In this approach a set of tasks is grouped to form a supertask T x and tasks comprising this supertask are called component tasks. Tasks that are not grouped to form a supertask are called migrating tasks. These supertasks among other migrating tasks are scheduled globally by a Pfair scheduling algorithm. Whenever a supertask is scheduled, its processor time is allocated to one of its component task according to an internal scheduling algorithm.

Supertasking effectively relaxes the strictness of Pfair scheduling: the group is required to make progress at a steady rate rather than individual tasks. Unfortunately, Moir and Ramamurthy [8] demonstrated that using an ideal weight assignment with a supertask cannot, in general, guarantee the timeliness of its component tasks. Holman [7] has developed criteria where supertasks are assigned weights more than their actual weight to provide timeline guarantees to component tasks. It provides guarantees to component tasks but at the cost of loss in schedulability bound.

This paper addresses issue of establishing a relationship between weight of a supertask and those of component tasks to provide timeline guarantees.We establish a condition which must be taken into account while constructing a supertask from component tasks. We prove that all component tasks will respect their timeline constraints, if supertask and its component tasks have the established relation/condition in them. Moreover the scheduling bound remains intact i.e M% The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: the following section presents the system model. In section 3, we explain some basics about global scheduling policy (Pfair) and local scheduling policies. In section 4 and 5 we develop the weight bound relation between supertask and its component task such that timeline constrains are guaranteed for component tasks. Section 6 describes exemptions in above mentioned conditions. An example is detailed in section 7. Conclusions are made in Section 8.

div.head: System Model
div.p: Consider a collection of periodic and synchronous real time tasks τ to be executed on a system of multiprocessor (M number of processors). The periodic task model of Liu and Layland [5] provides the simplest notion of a recurrent task. Each periodic task T is characterized by a period T.p, a relative deadline T.d, and an execution requirement T.e (T.e≤ T.d). Such a task is invoked every T.p time units, with its first invocation occurring at time t=0. We refer to each invocation of a task as a job, and the corresponding time of invocation as the job's release time. We assume in this paper that T.d = T.p, i.e., the relative deadline of a periodic task equals its period. Each job of τ requires at most T.e units of processor time to complete in each interval [k.T.p, (k+1).T.p) where k ≥ 0. In other words, each job must complete before the release of next job of the same task.

Following Baruah et al. [1] we refer wt(T) as weight or utilization of a task T which is the ratio of its execution requirement over its period, i.e. wt(T) = T.e/T.p . Because 0 < T.e ≤ T.p, we have 0 < wt(T) ≤ 1. The weight of a task determines the fraction (i.e. share) of a single processor that it requires. Following Baruah, we assume that processor time is allocated in discrete time units or quanta and execution requirement T.e and period T.p are integer multiples of this basic quanta.

We assume that all tasks are preemptive i.e. a task can be interrupted during its execution and can be resumed later from the same point. We assume that the overhead of preemption is zero. We further assume that all tasks are independent, i.e., the execution of a task is not affected by the execution of other tasks. In particular, we assume that tasks do not share any resources other than the processor, and that they do not self-suspend during their execution.

div.head: Exemptions
div.p: If the weight of component task and that of its corresponding supertask satisfy the condition 2A, then all component tasks are guaranteed to meet their deadline constraints. Component tasks are exempted from the second condition for which the following condition hold true. Two consecutive window tasks do not overlap at the period boundaries of the supertask. It implies that number of effective window tasks in interval [j.T i .p, (j+1).T i .p) is equal to number of such window tasks which have their release times and deadlines in the interval as well.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: We have demonstrated that in hierarchical scheduling policy where Pfair is used as a global scheduling policy, component tasks respect their deadlines if relation between weight of supertask and those of component tasks is as per condition 2.

We have formally established the sufficient condition to provide timeline guarantees to its component tasks i.e. minimum number of window tasks that a supertask T x must have (in specified interval). We have derived the relation to be held to provide these minimum number of window tasks in supertask. We have not introduced an inflation factor that minimizes the utilization of the system.
In future we are planning to develop heuristics to partition tasks on different processors while taking into account both conditions developed in this article.
